newsitem.title: UK: Forex intervention? Watch the economic background.
newsitem.headline: Forex intervention? Watch the economic background.

text.p: Intervention jitters are continuing to unsettle currency markets, but analysts say it is important to keep a close eye on the economic background and not get fixated by the forex foreground.
There is little doubt that central banks would step in if the dollar staged a dramatic surge, but currently there is probably little for traders to worry about.
Background economic conditions are more important than actual levels, analysts said on Thursday.

"Last weekend's G7 meeting was a statement of intent to do nothing," said Avinash Persaud, head of currency research at J.P. Morgan, in reference to the Berlin meeting of finance ministers and central bank chiefs from the seven leading industrialised nations.
"I don't think there is a level, I think there is a condition upon which they would act and it is different in every country."
Of the Group-of-Three -- U.S., Germany and Japan -- Japan is the most concerned about the strong dollar while the United States and Germany are more relaxed.
In fact they could actually be quite happy given the anti-inflation effect of a strong dollar in the U.S. and the help it gives exporters in Germany.
Japan is concerned about the impact a weak yen is having on stock prices and does not want to deter overseas investors, who are significant players on the stock market.

An ailing Japanese banking sector is not helped either by a weaker yen and falling stock prices. What matters to Japanese banks is yen- based capital so they are very concerned about the Nikkei falling.
In the United States it is the current account gap which might start to be a concern. A significant widening of the deficit might see the authorities get more concerned about the level of the dollar.
In Germany the most important figure to watch is imported inflation and in December import prices rose 0.8 percent.
"That is perhaps where the biggest danger is." Morgan's Persaud said. "Another few months like that and the Bundesbank will start to say the current level of dollar/mark is too high."

This would be dangerous for the market because when the dollar was declining -- between the first quarter of 1994 and the second quarter of 1995 -- its fall was only halted when Germany entered the fray along with the U.S. Federal Reserve to turn it round.
Prior to that the Bank of Japan (BoJ) bought hundreds of millions of dollars to no avail.

So even if the dollar remains static around current levels, which the authorities have described as "appropriate" , a deterioration in some economic figures could automatically make it look too high and the market should then watch out, analysts said.

"The philosophy has changed," Persaud said. "The Louvre accord had target ranges, they didn't tell us what they were but they had them, and now it's not really levels they are worried about it's the background conditions."

The Louvre accord of February 1987 resulted in the adoption of a package of policy commitments and exchange rate understandings among the Group of Seven (G7) -- the United States, Japan, Germany, Canada, Britain, France and Italy -- aimed at stabilising the dollar.
But at present holders of long dollar positions should be safe as long as the rise is not too rapid.

"I think G6 are quite prepared to see the dollar go higher but Japan has reached a stage where they are genuinely concerned about levels as opposed to rate of change," said Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica.

Japan's reserves built up to over $200 billion as it intervened during the dollar's fall so the Bank of Japan has plenty of ammunition and it is on dollar/yen where intervention is likely to come first, analysts said.
But they could not be too aggressive as any selling of dollar/yen will drain liquidity from the domestic banking system and lead to de facto monetary tightening that will hit growth.
"Assuming we get intervention it will first come unilaterally from Japan but after an initial big impact I wouldn't think it would have a lasting impact," Hawkins said.
"If the Bundesbank and Fed come in as well it would have a big impact but ultimately until the fundamental picture starts, changing the dollar probably wouldn't stay down."
